answer.rationale: The two measurable declines (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) point at the funnel stage, not at price. memory_73 explicitly records that aggressive price cuts bought signups and short-term revenue while costing 12 points of early retention, which is directly counter to the sustainable qualified-revenue objective, so promotional_pricing is excluded despite the competitor pressure. memory_57 (referral) and memory_44 (enterprise sales-assist) are real levers but neither addresses the observed regression. That leaves simplify_onboarding and activation_messaging; onboarding sits upstream of activation, so fixing completion plausibly recovers part of both metrics, whereas messaging only touches the downstream one. I verify memory_86 (the direct onboarding record, day 52, closest to the current regression) and memory_91 (the strongest alternative, so I can compare rather than confirm). Uncertainty I am carrying rather than collapsing: these memories are consolidated summaries with archived sources, none of them were run under a competitor price shock, memory_86 is 24 days old and memory_31 is 64 days old, and 'improved completion' is not the same claim as 'improved qualified revenue' — the lift may have been on a cohort mix that no longer exists. Downstream value risk is real and specific: memory_31's mechanism was cutting required signup fields, which can degrade lead qualification data, routing, and the enterprise demo-request path recorded in memory_44 — i.e. a completion-rate win that quietly converts qualified pipeline into unqualified volume. So I will instrument the test on qualified-revenue and retention outcomes, not on completion rate alone, and will not strip fields that feed enterprise routing. If verification shows memory_86's lift was measured only on completion with no revenue or retention follow-through, I switch to activation_messaging.
